title: DHS Formally Publishes $70,000-per-Student OPT Fee Proposal, Schools on Hook
excerpt: The rule moves from White House review to formal publication: universities — not students — would pay $70,000 per initial OPT application and $30,000 per renewal, totaling about $100,000 over three years. A 60-day comment period opens now, with lawsuits expected.
body:
• DHS formally published a proposed rule Wednesday: universities — not students — must pay $70,000 for each student's initial OPT application and $30,000 for each renewal or STEM extension.
  • Over the full three-year pathway, the fee per graduate totals about $100,000 — roughly 200 times the ~$500 students currently pay.
  • DHS says the fee will combat fraud and protect American workers, calling OPT a "pipeline for cheap foreign labor." Colleges, employers, and immigration lawyers predict lawsuits and warn it will push students to other countries.
  • What it means for you: A 60-day comment period is now open and lawsuits are near-certain, so nothing changes for enrolled students yet. But if US study with post-graduation work is in your plans, watch closely — at $70,000 a head, many universities may limit OPT sponsorship or pass costs on.

The Trump administration formally proposed making post-graduation work dramatically more expensive for international students: the Department of Homeland Security published a rule Wednesday requiring universities to pay $70,000 for every student enrolled in Optional Practical Training (OPT), the work program used by hundreds of thousands of foreign graduates each year. Publication moves the proposal out of White House review into formal rulemaking, with a 60-day comment period before it can be finalized. Students currently pay around $500, per Reuters.

What the rule proposes

Under the proposal, F-1 visa holders seeking OPT — which lets international students work in jobs related to their field during school or after graduation — would no longer pay the fee themselves. Schools would pay $70,000 per initial application and $30,000 per additional authorization. OPT allows up to 20 hours of work per week while school is in session and 12 months after graduation; STEM graduates can extend for another 24 months. DHS said the fee would "combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system, and protect US workers," with a spokesperson calling OPT a "back door" into the workforce.

https://x.com/instablog9ja/status/2107933979022139902

A wider crackdown on legal immigration

The proposal extends a pattern. In August, DHS proposed a $103,265 fee for new H-1B workers after an earlier $100,000 H-1B charge was blocked in court. USCIS Director Joseph Edlow has said he wants to eliminate post-graduation work through OPT entirely. Last year, thousands of students had their status abruptly terminated. New international enrollment fell 17% last fall, the sharpest drop since the pandemic, per the American Council on Education. The shift is striking against 2024 campaign pledges: Trump then said foreign graduates should automatically get a Green Card.

Who actually pays

Moving the fee to schools does not erase it; it lands on the institutions least able to absorb it. Houston immigration lawyer Steven Brown told the Associated Press the intent is transparent:

"I think this is the next level of attack, and I think it's a design to kill the program without killing the program. I don't see too many schools wanting to pay $70,000 for a student to get OPT."

— Steven Brown, immigration lawyer, to the Associated Press

Universities could cap OPT participation, decline sponsorship, or pass costs back to students. Business groups warn the fee would starve American employers of STEM graduates, and legal challenges are widely expected: Doug Rand of the Talent Mobility Fund predicted on LinkedIn that the rule "isn't going to fare well in the courts."

The Indian-student angle

For the diaspora, this strikes the single most-used legal pathway from US study to US work. Indian students are the largest national cohort of international students in the US, and OPT is the bridge that converts American tuition into H-1B careers for thousands of Indian graduates annually, overwhelmingly in STEM. A $100,000 cumulative fee makes them the costliest entry-level international cohort to employ, even as the H-1B route faces six-figure fees of its own.

"Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership."

— Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators

Indian families weighing crores in tuition against post-study work must now price in the chance that their university declines to sponsor OPT at all. With enrollment already falling, the US risks ceding the Indian-student market to Canada, the UK, and Australia, where post-study work routes remain comparatively open.

What's next

The 60-day comment period is open, and universities and business groups are expected to flood the docket with opposition — and sue the moment DHS moves toward finalization. Given the blocked H-1B fee and the halted four-year F-1 rule, the OPT proposal faces a long court fight before any fee is collected. Students currently in OPT or planning to enroll are unaffected until a final rule takes effect.
